strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK to Reduce Memory Stalls
strategy_description: Adding a @triton.autotune decorator with multiple XBLOCK and num_warps configurations allows the runtime to select the tile size that best hides memory latency. In this case, the before kernel had severe L1TEX scoreboard stalls (27.5 cycles/warp, 68.8% of CPI) and low issue slot utilization (37%); after autotuning, warp cycles per issued instruction dropped from ~40 to ~5 and issue slot utilization rose from 37% to 57%, yielding an 8.6% speedup. This strategy is most effective when the kernel is memory-latency-bound with high warp stall cycles and low eligible warps per scheduler, as larger or smaller XBLOCK values can change the instruction mix and latency hiding behavior.
slow_pseudocode:
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    # fixed XBLOCK=128 at call site
    ...

kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Triton kernel with fixed XBLOCK constexpr, high warp stall cycles due to L1TEX scoreboard dependencies (>20 cycles/warp), low issue slot utilization (<50%), and memory-bound workload (DRAM throughput >70%). The kernel grid is large enough that autotuning overhead is amortized.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel is compute-bound rather than memory-latency-bound; kernel has very small grid sizes where autotuning overhead dominates; XBLOCK is constrained by shared memory or correctness requirements that prevent exploration of larger tile sizes.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: use @triton.autotune with key=['xnumel'] (or the relevant problem-size dimension) so the autotuner caches the best config per problem size. num_stages controls software pipelining depth. Equivalent in CUDA would be launch-bound tuning or persistent kernel tile-size sweeps.
